abstract: <jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title><jats:p>Climate change, drought, and soil salinization present huge limitations to global agricultural output, which threatens food security. This necessitates the cultivation and domestication of wild edible halophytes as alternatives to mainstream food crops, especially in arid and semi‐arid regions. <jats:italic>Trachyandra ciliata</jats:italic> is one of the under‐researched and underutilized edible halophytes native to South Africa. The plant was used as a food source by Khoisan people in the past although its edibility and nutritional capacity are undocumented. Thus, the current study explored the effect of varying salinity concentrations on minerals, proximate, phytochemical, and anti‐nutrient composition of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"><jats:italic>T. ciliata</jats:italic></jats:styled-content> to evaluate its edibility and promote its cultivation among South African households. Plants were subjected to varying salinity treatments from 0, 50, 100,150, and 200 mM prepared by adding sodium chloride (NaCl) to the nutrient solution. Salinity significantly influenced the mineral, proximate, antinutrient, and phytochemical composition of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"><jats:italic>T. ciliata</jats:italic></jats:styled-content>. Control and 50 mM treatments recorded significantly higher macro and micronutrient content in the flower buds and leaves, except for heavy metals such as Zn and Cu, which increased with increasing salinity and significantly higher in the roots. Leaves under low salinity treatments recorded higher moisture and protein content, while leaves also recorded higher ash content under high salinity. On the other hand, flower buds under low salinity recorded significantly high fat and NDF composition. Phytochemicals and antinutrients increased with increasing salinity concentrations. The low antinutrient content and high nutritional, mineral and phenolic contents validate the edibility and suitability of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case"><jats:italic>T. ciliata</jats:italic></jats:styled-content> for human consumption.</jats:p>
title: Salinity Influenced Proximate, Minerals, Anti‐Nutrients and Phytochemical Composition of Trachyandra ciliata Kunth (Wild Cabbage): A Promising Edible Halophyte

abstract: <jats:p>Plant growth and productivity are predicted to be affected by rising CO2 concentrations, drought and temperature stress. The C3 crop model in a changing climate is Chenopodium quinoa Willd—a protein-rich pseudohalphyte (Amaranthaceae). Morphophysiological, biochemical and molecular genetic studies were performed on quinoa grown at ambient (400 ppm, aCO2) and elevated (800 ppm, eCO2) CO2 concentrations, drought (D) and/or high temperature (eT) treatments. Among the single factors, drought caused the greatest stress response, inducing disturbances in the light and dark photosynthesis reactions (PSII, apparent photosynthesis) and increasing oxidative stress (MDA). Futhermore, compensation mechanisms played an important protective role against eT or eCO2. The disruption of the PSII function was accompanied by the activation of the expression of PGR5, a gene of PSI cyclic electron transport (CET). Wherein under these conditions, the constant Rubisco content was maintained due to an increase in its biosynthesis, which was confirmed by the activation of rbcL gene expression. In addition, the combined stress treatments D+eT and eCO2+D+eT caused the greatest negative effect, as measured by increased oxidative stress, decreased water use efficiency, and the functioning of protective mechanisms, such as photorespiration and the activity of antioxidant enzymes. Furthermore, decreased PSII efficiency and increased non-photochemical quenching (NPQ) were not accompanied by the activation of protective mechanisms involving PSI CET. In summary, results show that the greatest stress experienced by C. quinoa plants was caused by drought and the combined stresses D+eT and eCO2+D+eT. Thus, drought consistently played a decisive role, leading to increased oxidative stress and a decrease in defense mechanism effectiveness.</jats:p>
title: Drought Has a Greater Negative Effect on the Growth of the C3 Chenopodium quinoa Crop Halophyte than Elevated CO2 and/or High Temperature

abstract: <jats:p>In order to determine how salinity and exposure time affect seed viability and germination, seeds of five halophytes, <jats:italic>Atriplex prostrata, Hordeum jubatum, Salicornia europaea, Spergularia marina,</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>Suaeda calceoliformis</jats:italic> were exposed to 3.0, 5.0, and 10.0% NaCl solutions for 30, 60, 90, 365, and 730 d. Recovery experiments in distilled water indicated significantly different species responses to salinity over time. Percentage germination and rate of germination in <jats:italic>H. jubatum</jats:italic> were dramatically reduced following extended exposure and all seeds exposed to 10% NaCl for > 1 yr failed to germinate. <jats:italic>Spergularia marina</jats:italic> seeds were stimulated following short‐term exposure to 3% NaCl; however, germination was delayed and overall germination was significantly reduced with exposure time in the two higher salinity levels. Percentage germination in <jats:italic>A. prostrata</jats:italic> decreased over time, but salinity level was not related to this reduction. Germination of <jats:italic>S. europaea</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>S. calceoliformis,</jats:italic> the most salt‐tolerant species being tested, was stimulated by exposure to high salinity. Both species had a significant increase in percentage germination and in the germination rate when compared to seeds germinated in distilled water. Baseline germination data from seeds placed in 0, 1, 2, and 3% NaCl solutions indicated that <jats:italic>S. europaea</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>S. calceoliformis</jats:italic> were the only species to germinate in the 3% NaCl solution. <jats:italic>Spergularia marina</jats:italic> failed to germinate in the 2% NaCl treatment, and germination of <jats:italic>A. prostrata</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>H. jubatum</jats:italic> was significantly reduced at this salinity level. It is concluded that prolonged exposure to saline solutions can inhibit or stimulate germination in certain species, and the resulting germination and recovery responses are related to the duration and intensity of their exposure to salt in their natural habitats.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title><jats:p>Two sympatric subspecies of the xerohalophyte <jats:italic>Atriplex canescens</jats:italic> Pursh. (Nutt.) were compared for 84 d in outdoor salinity trials in their native coastal desert environment in Sonora, Mexico. Subspecies <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> grows naturally on sea water in the high intertidal zone of estuaries while subspecies <jats:italic>canescens</jats:italic> grows on dunes. In lysimeter pot experiments, ssp. <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> exhibited 50% growth reduction when the mean root zone salinity reached 1160 mol m<jats:sup>−3</jats:sup> NaCl compared to just 760 mol m<jats:sup>−3</jats:sup> for ssp. <jats:italic>canescens.</jats:italic> When irrigated with sea water in a flood plot, ssp. <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> had 50% higher growth rates than ssp. <jats:italic>canescens.</jats:italic> The specialization of ssp. <jats:italic>linearis</jats:italic> for a saline environment was associated with greater net transport of Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> from root to shoot, greater Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> accumulation in the leaves and a higher Na:K ratio in the leaves compared to ssp. <jats:italic>canescens.</jats:italic> On the other hand, the two subspecies achieved approximately the same degree of osmotic adjustment in the leaves, equal to two to three times the external salinity, and had similar water use efficiencies. Even at relatively low salinities, both subspecies accumulated larger quantities of Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> for osmotic adjustment than K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>. The results suggest that breeding for Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> accumulation rather than exclusion might be the more effective strategy for improving salt tolerance of conventional crop plants.</jats:p>
title: How much sodium accumulation is necessary for salt tolerance in subspecies of the halophyte Atriplex canescens?

abstract: <jats:p>The importance of blue carbon is significant in terms of climate change mitigation and marine ecosystem conservation, and halophyte acts as a crucial reservoir for this blue carbon. Accordingly, this study utilized unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) optical sensors to create a distribution map of vegetation in the natural salt marsh of the Jujin estuary. The optical images captured from a UAV at an altitude of 50 m provide ultra-high-resolution optical information with a ground sampling distance of 0.6 cm. Based on these images, a U-Net model was trained to classify <i>Phragmites communis</i> and <i>Suaeda maritima</i>, generating a classification map of the mixed habitats of salt marsh plants. The areas of <i>Phragmites communis</i> and <i>Suaeda maritima</i> in the Jujin- Cheon region were found to be 6,653.23 m<sup>2</sup> and 1,409.08 m<sup>2</sup>, respectively. The classification results were validated using field control point data, confirming an approximate classification accuracy of 92%.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Little is known about how upper marsh plants (growing in freshwater) will respond physiologically to sudden increases in salinity. In this study, we used experimental microcosms to evaluate changes in plant-water relations in the halophyte <jats:italic>Spartina patens</jats:italic> following increases in soil salinity (salinity levels: 15, 30, and 45). There was a delay (by 3–5 weeks) in the lowering of leaf water potential (ψ<jats:sub>leaf</jats:sub>), stomatal conductance (g), and tissue water content (θ) in plants subjected to salinities of 30–45. These physiological delays in plant-water adjustments following sudden increases in salinity may be an adaptation of <jats:italic>S. patens</jats:italic> that allows it to effectively exploit higher habitat elevations that receive intermittent seawater inundations without promoting costly physiological modifications.</jats:p>
title: Delayed modifications in plant-water relations in the coastal marsh halophyte Spartina patens following sudden increases in soil salinity
